lead: Hippie style is the dress of the 1960s counterculture: long hair on men, beards, beads, feathers, flowers, bells and clothing drawn from folk, 19th-century American and Native American styles. It is a deliberate bohemian look defined by expressive, unstructured clothes rather than tailoring.
As a style choice it changes presentation through color, texture, accessories and hair, and it has been revived repeatedly at festivals and in fashion cycles.

paras: People assemble it from loose or flared garments, layered or patterned textiles, natural-looking fabrics, long or unstyled hair, flowers and handmade accessories such as beads. It is worn as an everyday style or for festivals.
No health risks come from the style. As with any strongly identified aesthetic, how it reads depends on setting and on the wearer's overall grooming.

angle.text: Hippie style changes how someone looks through clothing, hair and accessories alone, using patterns, layers and handcrafted items as its vocabulary [1].

lead: Hippie style is the countercultural, bohemian dress associated with the hippie movement of the mid to late 1960s. The most concrete image is a bearded person adorned with beads, feathers, flowers and bells, with long hair on men as a key marker [1].

As a look, it works through expressive, unstructured clothing, accessories and hair rather than fit and polish. Its roots include German Wandervogel youth dress, California 'Nature Boys', Beat and hipster styles, and 19th-century and Native American clothing [1].
No appearance research has tested hippie style as a looks strategy; its documentation is in cultural history.
infobox: Long hair, beads, flowers, folk textiles

paras: In 1961 the painter Vito Paulekas and his wife Szou opened a Hollywood boutique credited as among the first to introduce hippie fashion [1]. In 1965 'proto-hippies' at the Red Dog Saloon in Virginia City, Nevada, wore long hair, boots and clothing drawn from 19th-century American and Native American styles [1]. After San Francisco's Fox Theater closed in 1966, hippies bought its costume stock and dressed in it for ballroom performances [1].

In 1967 the Summer of Love and flower children popularized flowers in hair, and coverage of Haight-Ashbury made the look widely known [1]. From 1968 hippie-influenced fashion moved into the mainstream, with longer men's hair spreading widely, and the style spread to the UK, Europe, Australia, Canada, Mexico and Brazil [1]. By the early 1970s much of it had been absorbed into mainstream American dress [1].
Neo-hippies remain visible at festivals and gatherings, and the term 'Zippie' from about 1994 described hippies who embraced new technology and electronic music [1].
